title: Capecitabine
purpose: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.
schedule_summary: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.

agents.name: Capecitabine
agents.explanation: After you swallow capecitabine, your body changes it into fluorouracil. This interferes with the DNA and RNA processes cells use to grow. Normal cells can also be affected, which helps explain mouth soreness, bowel symptoms and changes in blood counts.
agents.watch: Stop tablets and contact the team for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth ulcers, hand-foot soreness affecting activities, fever or dehydration. Chest pain needs urgent assessment. Do not restart until instructed.
risks: Severe early toxicity, including DPD-related toxicity

chronology_notes.title: Your written plan comes first
chronology_notes.text: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.

chronology_notes.title: Symptoms can build
chronology_notes.text: Bowel, mouth and hand-foot symptoms may accumulate and can continue during tablet-free days.

chronology_notes.title: Act when symptoms occur
chronology_notes.text: Do not wait for the next visit or use the chart to decide a symptom is safe.

chronology_notes.title: Across the course
chronology_notes.text: The pattern can change between cycles. Dose changes and treatment breaks are made with the team.

day_groups.title: Treatment days
day_groups.body: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.
day_groups.action: Use the current tablet label. Swallow whole with water with or within 30 minutes of food; do not crush or cut tablets.

day_groups.title: Planned tablet-free days
day_groups.body: Do not take leftover tablets to replace doses missed earlier. Side effects may continue during this interval.
day_groups.action: Keep the oncology contact plan available and confirm the next review before restarting.

support.title: Nausea prevention and rescue
support.text: The team agrees a rescue medicine if needed; routine daily anti-sickness prevention is not automatically required for this oral low-risk schedule.

support.title: Bowel symptoms
support.text: Report diarrhoea promptly and follow the written rescue plan. Severe symptoms, fever, dehydration or inability to drink need urgent advice.

support.title: Counts and recovery
support.text: White-cell growth-factor injections are prescribed according to individual risk and previous complications. They are not automatically required for every patient or every cycle.

support.title: Skin and mouth care
support.text: Use gentle skin and mouth care. Painful hands and feet or mouth sores can require a tablet hold and team review; do not continue simply to finish the pack.

sections.title: Before the first treatment
sections.text: Confirm the aim, likely course length, blood-test arrangements and a working urgent contact number. DPD testing is required before starting the fluoropyrimidine unless already completed.

sections.title: Taking the tablets
sections.text: Use the prescribed morning and evening dose within 30 minutes after food on the agreed treatment days. Do not make up a missed or vomited dose. Follow the team’s hold instructions for significant diarrhoea, mouth soreness or painful hands and feet, and contact them promptly.

sections.title: If treatment is delayed
sections.text: Ask the unit to confirm the new treatment and blood-test dates. Re-anchor supportive medicines to the treatment actually given; do not take an extra or catch-up anticancer dose yourself.

sections.title: Getting help between visits
sections.text: Follow your oncology unit’s urgent advice for fever, infection, severe diarrhoea, chest pain or difficulty breathing. Bring your treatment card and current medicines list.

chapters.title: Your treatment aim and duration
chapters.intro: The same medicine can be used for different purposes.

items.title: Why this treatment?
items.text: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.

items.title: How long?
items.text: NCCP recommends six months / eight cycles for adjuvant colon or residual triple-negative breast cancer. For advanced disease, duration depends on response and tolerability.

items.title: Alternatives and decisions
items.text: Discuss the expected benefit, burdens, reasonable alternatives and the option of supportive care. The best choice depends on your cancer, fitness and preferences.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Tablets are active chemotherapy, with a specific schedule.

items.title: Meals and doses
items.text: Use your current prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water with or within 30 minutes after food. Do not cut, chew or crush them; ask pharmacy if swallowing is difficult.

items.title: Missed doses or vomiting
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. Never double the next dose. Contact the team for repeated vomiting or uncertainty about the schedule.

items.title: Pause and restart
items.text: Stop tablets for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth/hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, fever or dehydration and seek advice. A toxicity-related pause requires instructions before restart.

items.title: Different tablet strengths
items.text: Different strengths may be combined to make your dose. A reduction changes tablet numbers: use the new label and do not calculate a change from this page.

chapters.title: Tests and checks
chapters.intro: Monitoring helps the team decide whether treatment can continue.

items.title: DPD testing
items.text: DPD helps break down fluoropyrimidine medicines. Low activity can cause severe toxicity; testing before treatment helps guide the plan but cannot prevent every serious reaction.

items.title: Blood, kidney and liver results
items.text: Counts, kidney and liver function are checked before each cycle. Diarrhoea and poor intake can worsen kidney function and make tablets harder to tolerate.

items.title: Your symptoms matter
items.text: Report bowel frequency, stoma output, mouth soreness, hand-foot pain, chest symptoms and what daily activities you can no longer manage.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: The team sets the scan or follow-up plan for your particular treatment aim.

chapters.title: Recognise symptoms and act
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment if you feel unwell.

items.title: Bowel and hydration
items.text: Report diarrhoea or increased stoma output early. Inability to drink, dizziness, very little urine, severe pain or blood in stool needs prompt assessment.

items.title: Hands, feet and mouth
items.text: Pain, cracking, peeling or ulcers that affect normal activities or eating/drinking need advice. Gentle preventive care helps, but does not replace reporting.

items.title: Chest symptoms and infection
items.text: Stop capecitabine and seek urgent assessment for chest pain. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact, even if the temperature is normal.

items.title: Treatment-specific effects
items.text: Severe toxicity can happen early. Do not assume that tablets are mild treatment or that a normal DPD result makes symptoms safe to ignore.

chapters.title: Daily life and other medicines
chapters.intro: Make the plan fit your practical needs.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Aim for tolerable meals and fluids; contact the team if intake falls. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to your energy. Ask for dietetic help if needed.

items.title: Medicine and supplement checks
items.text: Check new medicines with oncology pharmacy. Warfarin can require closer INR checks; phenytoin levels may need monitoring. Brivudine is an important prohibited interaction.

items.title: Family, work and fertility
items.text: Ask about infection exposure, work, intimacy, contraception, fertility and any caring responsibilities. Use the medicine-specific duration of precautions given by your team.

items.title: Procedures and travel
items.text: Plan transport and support around appointments. Ask which symptoms or blood-count problems affect travel and when to contact the service.

chapters.title: Review, recovery and follow-up
chapters.intro: Your plan can change as treatment progresses.

items.title: Dose changes are individual
items.text: A pause or reduction may be needed because of symptoms, blood results or kidney function. The team considers the treatment aim and other options.

items.title: After the last dose
items.text: Keep reporting new or persistent symptoms after treatment ends. Your team confirms follow-up, scans and recovery support; the timeline is not a forecast.

items.title: Prepare for review
items.text: Bring questions, symptoms and missed-dose records. Tell the team what matters most to you and ask them to explain the next decision.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.

questions.q: Which days do I take the tablets?
questions.a: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.

questions.q: What if I forget a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next planned dose at its usual time unless treatment has been stopped; report repeated vomiting and check with the team if unsure.

questions.q: When should I stop tablets and call?
questions.a: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Do not restart after a toxicity interruption until the team advises.

questions.q: Why do I need blood tests if I take tablets at home?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney and liver results, together with symptoms, guide whether to continue and at what dose.

questions.q: Do I need a port or a pump?
questions.a: No take-home chemotherapy pump is used. Capecitabine is swallowed, so a central line is not required just to give it.
Ask for your review and follow-up plan. Continue reporting symptoms after the last dose; further therapy depends on the treatment aim and response.

anatomy: Painful ulcers or reduced intake: stop tablets and call.
New chest pain: stop tablets and seek urgent assessment.
Significant diarrhoea, increased output or dehydration needs prompt advice.
Pain or peeling affecting daily activity: stop tablets and call.
Fever, shivers or sudden illness: contact oncology immediately.
Reduced urine, dizziness or inability to drink needs assessment.
Report fatigue that prevents usual activities or self-care.
Severe early diarrhoea, mouth soreness or sudden illness needs urgent review.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Ask which evidence matches your cancer, treatment aim and medicines.
evidence.interpretation: In stage III colon cancer after surgery, capecitabine was at least as effective as the intravenous fluorouracil schedule studied. This comparison does not measure benefit against no treatment, and does not estimate benefit for breast cancer or cancer that has spread.

administration_text: Capecitabine 1250 mg/m² twice daily on Days 1–14 every 21 days.
